transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. What brings you in to see me?

Well, my husband thought I should come talk to someone, but really it’s this kitchen situation. It’s been going on close to two years now, and I know the contractor and a few people on our block have been working together somehow—quietly, you know, not out in the open—to cheat us and keep the kitchen half-wrong on purpose.

My husband keeps showing me receipts and saying, “See, this is what we paid for,” and they all have excuses, but receipts don’t explain why things keep ending up wrong in the same way. I mean, I’ve lived in that house a long time, I know when something isn’t right. And the neighbors, they act friendly, but you can tell when people know more than they’re saying.
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people around you don't seem to notice or hear?

I don’t think so… I mean, houses make noises, you know, pipes and the refrigerator clicking on, especially at night. Sometimes my husband sleeps right through things and I’ll say, “Did you hear that?” but that doesn’t mean it’s a voice or anything.

Seeing things—no, not like people standing there that aren’t there. My eyes aren’t what they used to be, and if the light is funny I might think something is on the counter, but then it’s just a towel or whatever. So… no, not really, not in the way you’re asking, I don’t think.

Over the past two years, have you noticed any extended periods—say, two weeks or more—where your mood, energy, or sleep changed dramatically, such as feeling extremely depressed and hopeless, or unusually elated, energetic, and needing little sleep?

I don’t know that I’d say dramatic. I mean, I get upset about the kitchen, of course I do—anyone would, after this long. And sleep, well, some nights I’m thinking about the cabinets or what the neighbors must have noticed, and then the next morning I’m tired.

But two weeks like you’re saying… extremely depressed or, what was the other one, elated? No, I don’t think of it that way. It’s more that the whole thing has been wearing, and then you have regular life on top of it—laundry, bills, my sister calling about her yard, all that. I’m not sure if that’s what you mean.

Aside from the concerns about the kitchen and neighbors, how have things been going in other areas of your life—like your relationships with friends and family, or your ability to manage daily responsibilities?

Oh, other than that, I’m… I’m pretty much doing what I usually do. I still go to church things, when they have the ladies’ gathering or the potluck—last week someone brought that lemon cake, though it was too sweet if you ask me. And I’ve got my book club, though half the time they pick these gloomy books and then wonder why nobody finishes them.

At home I keep up with the regular things, you know, laundry, meals, paying bills, making sure we don’t forget family plans. My family still sees me, we still do what we do. So it’s not like I’m just sitting in a chair all day. It’s really the remodel business that keeps intruding on everything.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (belief that a contractor and neighbors are conspiring to cheat her on a home remodel) persisting for nearly two years. There are no hallucinations, no evidence of thought disorder, and no manic or depressive episodes meeting duration/severity criteria. Functioning outside the delusional theme (household management, social engagements, relationships) remains intact, which argues against schizophrenia (where functional decline and broader psychotic symptoms are expected) and against a mood disorder with psychotic features (no mood episode identified). The circumscribed, systematized nature of the delusion, absence of hallucinations, and preserved global functioning are classic for Delusional Disorder (F22).
